solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Way t' inn glass is swirled round obliquely

indicators.note: glass contents swirled round are churned up, so the preceding letters get stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A drinker at the inn twirls a glass, perhaps a little the worse for wear.
explanation.walkthrough: The dialect 't'' for 'the' supplies a lone T to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Slantingways is an adverb meaning on the slant, at an angle, which is what moving obliquely means.

clue.text: Work loading Murphy's spade, dotty

indicators.note: loading means putting a cargo inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: a loy is a narrow Irish spade; Murphy stands for an Irishman
OP, short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: An Irish labourer shovelling with his spade seems a bit crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: A loy is the long narrow Irish spade; 'Murphy' is a stock name signalling Irish. OP sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Loopy is informal slang for crazy or eccentric, a synonym of dotty.

clue.text: Unacceptable idea I abandoned (5, two words)

indicators.note: something abandoned is left behind, so the letter named before it drops out

explanation.surface: An idea is dropped because it could not be accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the I from NOTION to leave two words, NOT ON.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Not on' is a British colloquial phrase meaning not permissible or out of the question.

clue.text: Misguided turn holding everything up concerning church council

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top
holding means having something inside it, so one piece sits within the other
misguided means led astray, so the letters wander out of order

explanation.surface: A wrong turn brings the whole procession to a halt on the way to a church gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trullan Council of 692 met in the domed hall (trullus) of the palace in Constantinople.
explanation.definitionFit: Trullan is the adjective for the Council in Trullo, the Quinisext ecumenical council of the Eastern Church.

clue.text: Imperial, fuzzy on chin, Henry trimmed — see monarch in it

indicators.note: in it tells us to place the monarch inside the jumbled letters
fuzzy means blurred or indistinct, so the letters are jumbled
trimmed means cut away, so the letter standing for Henry is taken out

explanation.surface: A description of an emperor's stubbly chin, freshly shaved, with a nod to a portrait of royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: H is the symbol for henry, the unit of inductance. Remove it from ONCHIN, jumble the rest, and put ER inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Neronic means like the emperor Nero, so it is an imperial adjective in the sense of belonging to an emperor.

clue.text: Yule warmer consumed in gallons

indicators.note: consumed in means swallowed up by, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: G is gallon; the plural doubles it
a Yule log is burnt to warm the house at Christmas

explanation.surface: A Christmas drink that people get through by the gallon.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: glogg is a Christmas drink downed in quantity, while the Yule log is the fire's warmer.
explanation.definitionFit: Glogg is Scandinavian hot spiced wine served at Christmas, a festive warming drink.

clue.text: What's exhibited prominently in women and men equally?

definitions.text: What's exhibited prominently in women and men equally?

indicators.note: what is shown most prominently is at the front, so the leading letters of the following words are taken

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A wry question about which bodily feature sticks out in both sexes.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes a paunch, which can protrude in anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Wame is a Scots and northern word for the belly, which in many people protrudes.

clue.text: Place for smokers in the Wild Boar & Hart

indicators.note: wild means untamed and disordered, so the letters run loose into a new order

parts.note: the ampersand is ignored; the two animal names are the fodder

explanation.surface: A pub called the Wild Boar & Hart has a smoking area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smokers' are not tobacco users but smoked fish: Arbroath smokies are hot-smoked haddock.
explanation.definitionFit: Arbroath is the Scottish fishing town famous for its smokies, so it is the home of these smoked fish.

clue.text: Close-fitting number female threads intricately, special

indicators.note: intricately means in a complicated, interwoven way, so the letters are tangled up

explanation.surface: A tight dress made of intricately worked special thread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is fashion talk for an outfit or garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath dress is a figure-hugging dress, and a number is an item of clothing in fashion jargon.

clue.text: Once exhausted in mood line retreats

indicators.note: in places the reversed line inside the word for mood
retreats means goes back, so the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone feeling drained watches a queue shuffle backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Toworne is an obsolete past participle meaning worn out or exhausted.

clue.text: One aims for high-flying discs, keeping rhythm initially in drums and horn

indicators.note: keeping means holding within, so the single letter goes inside the drums

parts.note: to tap is to drum the fingers

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of the word is kept

parts.note: a hooter is a horn, as on a car

explanation.surface: Describes a band whose drummer and horn player keep the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'high-flying discs' are clay pigeons, not records.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapshooter fires at clay pigeons flung into the air from a trap.

clue.text: Face group of old wiseacres one short (not the last)?

indicators.note: one short means lacking a single one, so the numeral one is taken away
not the last means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: the Seven Sages of ancient Greece, with the seven as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about one face among a band of old know-alls.
explanation.walkthrough: The Seven Sages were seven wise men of ancient Greece. Drop an I to make six, then drop the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: A visage is a person's face, a literary synonym.

clue.text: Source for grub

definitions.meaning: first meaning: origin, the thing from which something grows
second meaning: as a verb, to dig or rummage about

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like food or a larva, but it is the verb to dig, as pigs do.
explanation.definitionFit: Root means origin as a noun, and as a verb means to rummage or dig, like grubbing.

clue.text: Thick coat, black one pinched by crook

indicators.note: pinched by means gripped by, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: crome is a dialect word for a hook or crook
B, abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A thief has made off with a dark winter coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crook' is not a criminal but a hooked stick, crome in dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: A Crombie is a heavy woollen overcoat, named after the Scottish cloth maker.

clue.text: Palio out of control? It may bring about termination

indicators.note: out of control means running wild, so the letters break out of their order

parts.note: the Palio is the famous horse race in Siena

explanation.surface: The Siena horse race spirals out of control and might have to be called off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Termination' means ending a pregnancy, not a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiol, an oil from parsley, was formerly used as an abortifacient, so it can end a pregnancy.

clue.text: Local troops? Many lost, nation gripped by call for help

indicators.note: gripped by means held inside, so the shortened nation sits within the call
lost means gone missing, so the word many is removed from the nation's name

explanation.surface: Soldiers have suffered heavy losses and the country is crying out for aid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' marks a dialect word; 'Many lost' is not about casualties but an instruction to drop those letters from the nation's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Soger is a dialect form of soldier, so sogers are soldiers or troops.

clue.text: Given rise, I had task round college, well-defined

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I had

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the task wraps the college

parts.note: a stint is an allotted task

explanation.surface: A student recalls an assignment set around college that was clearly defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinct means clearly marked out or well-defined, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Invasion craft? Number stuffing loot bag freely

indicators.note: freely means without restraint, so the letters are loose to rearrange
stuffing means being packed inside, so the number goes in

parts.note: the letters of loot bag rearranged

explanation.surface: Raiders pack a sack of plunder for the voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is an example: Vikings invaded in longboats.
explanation.definitionFit: A longboat is the Viking warship used for raids and invasions.

clue.text: Bandages head of san applied to artist? Not so

indicators.note: not so means without so, so those two letters drop off the artist
head of means the first letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: first letter of san, a sanatorium

explanation.surface: A sanatorium patient's dressings are put on a painter, who denies it.
explanation.definitionFit: A spica is a figure-of-eight bandage, overlapping like an ear of grain, so spicas are bandages.

clue.text: Jock's pinched, from seven days in the highlands occupying filthy hole

indicators.note: occupying means sitting inside, so the week goes in the hole

parts.note: a pit is a dirty hole
ouk is the Scots word for week

explanation.surface: A Scot complains that a week in the Highlands has left him in a grubby hovel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jock' marks a Scots word, as does 'in the highlands'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poukit is Scots for pinched in the sense of thin and puny, peaky-looking.

clue.text: Protective part of parapet, thick round centre of course

indicators.note: round means encircling, so the thick word surrounds the middle letters
centre of means only the middle letters of the following word are kept

parts.note: the middle two letters of course

explanation.surface: A fortification's sturdy wall rings the centre of a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: In fortification a surtout is a raised part of a parapet giving cover from enfilading fire.

clue.text: Weak ninny given nutritious cereal and hard cheese

parts.note: a sap is a feeble fool
sago is a starchy food from palm pith

explanation.surface: A wimp gets fed porridge; tough luck for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cheese' sounds like British slang for bad luck, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapsago is a hard green Swiss cheese flavoured with clover.

clue.text: Dhobi service was carried out in local garden?

indicators.note: carried out means removed, so the word was is lifted out from the middle

parts.note: a bagwash is a laundry service where washing is sent in a bag; a dhobi is an Indian washerman

explanation.surface: An Indian washerman did the laundry in a local garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' here means in India, where a bagh is a garden; the question mark flags that locality.
explanation.definitionFit: Bagh is an Anglo-Indian word for a garden or orchard.

clue.text: Colt maybe, what no cowboy could do without?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a colt is a young example of the animal, in Western speech

definitions.text: what no cowboy could do without?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the mount a cowboy rides

explanation.walkthrough: 'Colt' tempts as the revolver, but here it is a young horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoss is the American Western dialect form of horse, the animal a cowboy depends on.

clue.text: On edge, a hundred runs short

indicators.note: short means lacking, so the letter for runs is left out

parts.note: a cantred is an old division of a county, a hundred

explanation.surface: A batsman nervously stuck in the nineties, a century just out of reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hundred runs' suggests cricket, but a hundred is an old county subdivision, in Wales and Ireland a cantred.
explanation.definitionFit: Canted means tilted or set on edge, at a slant.

clue.text: Leave behind jaunt after moving to US

indicators.note: moving means shifting about, so the letters change places

parts.note: the letters of to US rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone emigrates to America and leaves the past behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the jaunt behind the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstrip is to outrun or leave behind, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Rear of boat I am attached to — or was

definitions.text: Rear of boat I am attached to — or was

indicators.note: rear of means the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A helmsman fondly speaks of his place at the stern, past or present.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the helm, fixed at the rear of the boat; 'or was' marks the word as obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: Timon is an obsolete word for a helm or rudder, the steering gear at a boat's stern.

clue.text: Volume, old, kept in private room, an allurement

indicators.note: kept in means held inside, so the two short pieces go into the room

parts.note: a den is a private retreat

explanation.surface: An old book hidden in a study holds a strange attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allurement' is literal: a lure for catching fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A devon, or devon minnow, is an artificial spinning bait that lures fish.

clue.text: Rising in a state I released displays of peevishness

indicators.note: in a state means agitated or disordered, so the remaining letters are jumbled
released means let go, so the letter I is set free from the word

explanation.surface: Someone gets agitated and lets go in a fit of temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' looks like an up-pointer in a down clue but is simply the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Girns are snarls or grimaces of complaint, from the Scots verb to girn, to whine or show the teeth.

clue.text: Interfere in sleep skipping piano pieces, we hear?

indicators.note: skipping means missing out, so the piano letter is left off

parts.note: kip is British slang for sleep

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by its sound, not spelling

explanation.surface: Someone's nap is disturbed by snatches of piano music overheard.
explanation.definitionFit: To kibitz is to meddle or offer unwanted advice, from Yiddish, so it means to interfere.

clue.text: Souse as of old was barking (not quite all there)

indicators.note: not quite all there means slightly incomplete, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: a dog that bayed was barking

explanation.surface: An old-time drunk was raving mad and plainly not all there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' suggests barking mad, but it is a dog's bark; 'Souse' is to drench, not a drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Baye is an obsolete Spenserian word meaning to bathe or drench, which is to souse.

clue.text: St Andrews student from Italy in first half of term

indicators.note: in puts the country letter inside the shortened term
first half of means only the opening half of the word survives

parts.note: a semester is an academic term
I, international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: An Italian exchange student arrives at St Andrews early in the academic year.
explanation.walkthrough: St Andrews is Scotland's oldest university, with its own names for each year group.
explanation.definitionFit: At St Andrews a semie is a second-year student, a term peculiar to that university.

clue.text: SA bird forming part of nest in a mound

indicators.note: forming part of means the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: the letters run across nest, in, a and mound

explanation.surface: A South American bird builds its nest in a heap of earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The tinamou is a ground-dwelling South American bird related to the ratites; SA is South America.

clue.text: Section of Baudelaire, not his first in speech units

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letter is taken away from the speech units

parts.note: his points back to the French poet, whose first letter this is

explanation.surface: A passage from the French poet, built from units of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His' refers back to Baudelaire, so his first letter is the one dropped. 'Speech units' are parts of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Vers is French for verse or a line of poetry, so a section of a French poet's work.

clue.text: Defrocks unruly nuns about to leave, weak

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters wrap the other pieces
unruly means disorderly, so the letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: Disorderly nuns about to quit are too feeble to resist being stripped of office.
explanation.definitionFit: To ungown is to strip of a gown, so to deprive of clerical office, which is to defrock.

clue.text: One favouring capital punishment (twitching on tree it isn't!)

indicators.note: twitching means jerking about, so the letters jerk into a new order

explanation.surface: A grim aside on hanging: the body twitching on the tree, which the supporter denies.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket mocks the retentionist's view by picturing a hanged body twitching on a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A retentionist wants the death penalty retained, as opposed to an abolitionist.
